extracted.intended_audience: systematic review authors, Cochrane review teams, medical/healthcare librarians and information specialists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, documenting, assessing, and implementing bibliographic searches and the study-selection process for Cochrane (intervention) systematic reviews, including stopping rules, performance assessment, documentation, duplicate-report handling, reviewer workflows, and use of software/automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding when to stop developing the search
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often difficult to decide in a scientific or objective way when a search is complete and search strategy development can stop; the ability to decide when to stop typically develops through experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions for stopping rules include: stop if adding a series of new terms yields no new relevant records; stop if precision falls below a particular cut-off; stop when removal of terms/concepts results in missing relevant records; consider the amount of evidence already accrued (be more cautious when evidence is scarce). Document the reasons for stopping. Note that there has been little formal evaluation of stopping approaches and experience/ judgement is required. For living reviews different approaches to stopping have been suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing search sensitivity/performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether a strategy is performing adequately by checking whether the search finds publications recommended as key publications or those included in other similar reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough for a strategy to find only known records (this may indicate bias). Use citation searches and reference checking as checks of strategy performance. If citation/reference searching finds documents that the database searches had already retrieved (but were not known in advance), this suggests adequate performance. Use an evidence-based checklist such as the PRESS Evidence-Based Checklist to assess whether the search strategy is adequate (see Section 4.4.8). If PRESS dimensions are missing or raise concerns, the search may not be complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical techniques to assess search performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical techniques such as capture–recapture (capture-mark-recapture) and relative recall can be used to assess search performance and help decide when to stop searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture–recapture can estimate the number of missed studies and may inform stopping once cut-offs are identified; it requires results from at least two searches and may entail iterative searching/selection. Relative recall requires a range of searches so eligible studies are built up, then assesses how many eligible studies indexed in a database are found by that database’s search; useful near the end of the search process. These techniques need further prospective evaluation but can inform judgments about completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use citation searches to evaluate completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation searches, conducted using the included (eligible) studies identified after searches, may reveal additional relevant studies and serve as a measure of completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If citation searches yield many additional relevant records, the original searches may not have been optimal and should be revisited. Guidance on terminology, application, and reporting of citation searching has been published (TARCiS). Citation searching is also discussed as a cross-check alongside reference checking and other complementary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping searches for qualitative evidence by saturation
rubrics_metrics.description: In evidence synthesis involving qualitative data, searching is often more organic and intertwined with analysis and searching stops when new information ceases to be identified (saturation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document reasons for stopping and provide explanations/justifications centered around saturation. See the chapter on qualitative evidence for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting the search process (MECIR C36 - Documenting the search process) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document the search process in enough detail to ensure that it can be reported correctly in the review; searches of all resources should be reproducible to the extent possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document internal record-keeping (distinct from reporting in the review). Record sources searched, when, by whom, and which terms were used. For Cochrane reviews, copy and paste bibliographic database search strategies exactly as run into supplementary material, with search set numbers and total records retrieved. Do not re-type strategies. Specify the interface used (introductory/advanced) where relevant. Save offline copies in text format; screenshots may be necessary for some databases. Document searches of non-database sources (contacting experts/manufacturers, reference list searching, website scans) including terms used; these details can be put in an appendix and used for future updates. Record correspondence and summarise it in a search narrative describing major decisions shaping the strategy. Save locally/web-archived copies of internet information (e.g. WebCite) because web content changes. When web search results are too large to screen, report the number actually screened rather than the total number retrieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow PRISMA-S and PRISMA reporting recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Report full search strategies for all databases, registers and websites searched (PRISMA-S and PRISMA 2020 recommendations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRISMA-S provides details and examples to report search methods and information sources clearly and reproducibly. PRISMA 2020 changes recommend presenting full search strategies for all databases (not just at least one). Also follow PRISMA guidance on data availability statements (item 27) and track records/PRISMA flow diagram recommendations. Consider proposed data structures for transparent bibliographic searching reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve medical/healthcare librarians and information specialists early
rubrics_metrics.description: Review authors should seek guidance from a medical/healthcare librarian or information specialist at the earliest opportunity and such specialists should draft or comment on the search strategy sections prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Librarian co-authored reviews are associated with lower risk of bias. For Cochrane reviews, information specialists are expected to participate in drafting/commenting the search strategy. Early involvement improves documentation, strategy development, and reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat studies (not reports) as the unit of interest and collate multiple reports (MECIR C42) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cochrane review is a review of studies that meet eligibility criteria; each study may be reported in several articles/abstracts/reports, so collate multiple reports so each study — not each report — is the unit of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link multiple reports of the same study and use information from all reports to determine study eligibility. Do not assume one report per study. Choose and justify which report is the primary source for study results; do not discard secondary reports since they may contain additional outcomes/design information. Detect duplicate publications via trial IDs (NCT, ISRCTN, UTN), author names, location/setting, intervention details, participant numbers/baseline data, and study dates/duration. Correspond with study authors/investigators when uncertainties remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical stepwise process for selecting studies
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical process: merge search results, remove duplicate records, screen titles/abstracts (be over-inclusive), retrieve full texts, link multiple reports, examine full-text reports against eligibility criteria, correspond with investigators as needed, make final inclusion decisions, tag ongoing/incomplete studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide when to map records to studies. If data remain incomplete/unobtainable, tag studies as incomplete and list them in ‘Characteristics of studies awaiting classification’. Make decisions about ongoing studies for inclusion in ongoing studies table or included/awaiting classification tables depending on eligibility. Note that studies should not be omitted solely because outcome data are not reported (see MECIR C40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include studies irrespective of whether outcome data are reported in a usable way (MECIR C40) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include studies in the review irrespective of whether measured outcome data are reported in a ‘usable’ way; do not exclude studies solely because outcome data are not reported in a usable format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding studies for unusable outcome reporting may introduce bias due to selective outcome reporting and undermine the review. While such studies cannot be included in meta-analyses, consider implications of their omission. Studies may legitimately be excluded if outcomes were not measured. Adverse effect outcomes may present different issues due to larger pools of studies and difficulties assessing measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use at least two people independently for inclusion decisions and predefine resolution process (MECIR C39) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (at least) two people working independently to determine whether each study meets eligibility criteria; define in advance how disagreements will be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate selection reduces mistakes and bias. Final determination of eligibility based on full text must be duplicate; initial title/abstract screening can be single-person but duplicate is desirable. Pilot test eligibility criteria on a sample (6-8 articles including definite/possible/not eligible) to refine criteria and train reviewers. Experts may be biased; include at least one person not content-expert where advantageous. Resolve disagreements by discussion, arbitration by a third person if needed, or classify as awaiting assessment if additional information is required. Assess eligibility criteria in order of importance so one 'no' can be primary reason for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document selection decisions to enable flow diagram and excluded studies table (MECIR C41) (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document the selection process in sufficient detail to complete a flow diagram and a table of ‘Characteristics of excluded studies’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep track of numbers of references and subsequently the number of studies to construct the PRISMA-style flow diagram. Document reasons for exclusions for studies that a reader might reasonably expect to find in the review. Use reference management software, spreadsheets, or specialist review software to track decisions and reasons for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a focused ‘Characteristics of excluded studies’ list
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a list of excluded studies that details the specific reason for exclusion for any studies a reader might plausibly expect to see among the included studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list should be as brief as possible; do not list all reports identified by extensive searches or studies that obviously do not meet eligibility criteria (e.g. non-randomized when only randomized trials are eligible). For each excluded study include at least one explicit reason for exclusion. The list should cover studies that on the surface appear to meet eligibility criteria but do not on further inspection, or well-known studies likely to be thought relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map records to studies carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors will need to decide when to map records (individual reports) to studies (the underlying trial/research) if multiple records refer to one study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of included and excluded studies must be based on studies rather than records. During flow-diagram construction, match records to studies so numbers and reasons are correctly attributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate software/tools for managing study selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use productivity tools or purpose-built systems to manage selection when large numbers of records are identified; consider compatibility with other review software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covidence and EPPI-Reviewer are Cochrane-preferred tools with strong RevMan integration; EndNote X7 can be used with special methods. Identify software via catalogs like the Systematic Review Toolbox (note availability changes). Consider software that supports multiple concurrent users and integrates with review workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automation and machine learning cautiously for selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tools (AI, machine learning, text mining) can reduce workload substantially but must be used with caution and awareness of possible reductions in sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-learned classifiers (e.g. RCT Classifier) and workflows (Screen4Me with Cochrane Crowd) can identify RCTs and reduce screening burden. Active learning can prioritize records for screening. Evidence suggests automation can reduce manual screening by 30%–90% but sometimes at a cost of up to 5% sensitivity loss. Automatic elimination of records is not recommended for Cochrane reviews until safe stopping rules are validated; however, prioritization and semi-automation are useful. Emerging LLM-based tools may offer advantages but lack large valid evaluations as of mid-2023. Automation is promising for living reviews and evidence surveillance (e.g., COVID-19 case studies). Use natural language processing tools to highlight PICO elements/characteristics to support screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening workflows and shared resources (e.g. Screen4Me, Cochrane Crowd, RCT Classifier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where available, use established screening workflows and community resources to improve screening efficiency (e.g. Screen4Me, RCT Classifier, Cochrane Crowd).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen4Me incorporates the RCT Classifier and Cochrane Crowd to identify RCTs in authors' search results; Cochrane review teams can access the workflow via the Cochrane Register of Studies and should liaise with their Cochrane Group to use it. Reported workload reduction varies by domain; internal evaluations report mean reductions ~53% (range 26%–84%). Use guidance from the Cochrane Information Specialists’ Handbook for implementing these workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot test eligibility criteria and order criteria by importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilot eligibility criteria on a sample of reports to refine and clarify criteria and ensure consistent application; assess eligibility criteria in order of importance so the first 'no' can be used as the primary reason for exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot with a mix of definitely eligible, definitely not eligible, and doubtful reports. Training and calibration through piloting improve consistency across reviewers. Ordering criteria helps provide a single primary reason for exclusion and streamlines assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and archive web-found and time-varying information
rubrics_metrics.description: Save local or archived copies of internet-found information (ongoing/unpublished trials, web content) because web content and search engine algorithms change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store local copies in structured ways to allow retrieval. Use web-archiving tools (e.g. WebCite) where appropriate. Note that web searches are less reproducible; report the number actually screened when it is impractical to screen all retrieved results.
